summary: Grassy Knoll, Skamania County WA: 10-ft L-4 cab built 1934, replaced 1952, rebuilt after a 1953 windstorm, then gone; a hike to a meadow with lookout remnants reported.

facts.design: 10-foot wooden L-4 cab (1934); 1952 replacement cab of 15 or 20 feet, depending on source
facts.status_note: No standing lookout is described. The sources give no date for when the rebuilt cab was removed or destroyed.

access.note: Reached by a hiking trail from a dirt road with potholes, per WillhiteWeb. No closure is described in the sources read.

visit.trail_note: The trail starts in a meadow and climbs the ridge. WillhiteWeb puts the first knoll at 1.5 miles, with the main knoll after more ups and downs.

events.note: 10-foot wooden L-4 cab, about 2.5 miles southeast of the Big Huckleberry lookout
Replacement cab 15 feet per FFLOS; 20 feet per firelookout.com and WillhiteWeb
High winds blew the station down and demolished it. One June 1953 article says 'last year' (1952); another says January 1953.
Rebuilt in June 1953 as a 14-foot-square building, with materials dropped by parachute and the timbers packed in by mule

corrections.why: No fetched source gives a tower height. The sources give cab sizes of 10 feet (1934) and 15 or 20 feet (1952), and none gives 500 feet.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: FFLOS says a 15-foot L-4 replaced the 1934 cab in 1952. firelookout.com and WillhiteWeb say 20 feet. The story reports both.
A June 13, 1953 article says the station was blown down 'last year'. A June 28, 1953 article says the windstorm came in January 1953. The story reports both.
FFLOS, firelookout.com and WillhiteWeb date the replacement to 1952, but the June 1953 articles describe the rebuild that month. The story gives both.

sources.title: Grassy Knoll, Forest Lookouts (quoting The Oregonian, June 1953)

notes_for_editor: Read the four source pages (one page re-read with a different grep, so 5 reads of distinct pages plus one repeat) and ran 1 web search. The 'today' section rests on WillhiteWeb alone; its photo captions are dated 2015 and the page is otherwise undated. Access is marked public from a hiking description, not an agency notice; a Forest Service trail listing would confirm it. The brief's elevation_m 1112.2 was not checked against a fetched page; a 1953 article calls the knoll a '4500-foot peak'. Not used in the story.
